We talk a bit about R-square and adjusted R-square. R-square, in the formula, is actually highly correlated to mean square error because it measures the variance. Okay, so I'm going to talk about the first error, Mean Absolute Error. If you look at the formula, Mean Absolute Error, basically, there's an absolute sign here, and we are basically taking the target value, the actual prediction, minus your predicted value, and we take an absolute value. This absolute value will basically nullify the direction of your prediction, whether you're underestimating or overestimating. And what we do is we take an average. So, why is it that people choose to use MAE? Sometimes it's because MAE is very easy to interpret. From a business standpoint, MAE is very easy to interpret. I'm just taking a difference between my prediction, I take the absolute value, and I take the average. So it's the average, or rather, the mean absolute error. Basically, on average, how far I'm wrong. So one reason why you might want to choose this is because it's very easy to interpret. However, the metric, as you can see, Mean Absolute Error, is actually quite robust to outliers. And in order to maximize mean absolute error, usually if you predict the median, mean absolute error would love it. Because mean absolute error, you can see later on when we start to contrast with mean square error, you can see that mean absolute error is more robust to outliers as compared to mean square error.

This is the one that we talk about. Essentially, rather than take an absolute value, now you're just basically squaring the error. And in your head, you'll be thinking, why do I want to square the error? So, if you look at an error profile, mean square error actually looks like that. It's actually a curved shape. As the error starts to get larger, the intuition here is that when you try to square the error, errors that are very large will be very huge. So what this means is that the larger your error is, the larger it gets amplified. If your difference is 2, your error is actually going to be a 4. But if, let's say, it's a 10, 10 becomes 100. So you can start to see that the error basically starts to increase exponentially. So what this means is that if you were to choose to use MSE, it is going to be very sensitive to outliers. If your model were to make any bad prediction, the model will be forced to emphasize, will be forced to focus on that, because the cost of me making a very big mistake is going to be huge. So I'm rather, if I can focus on correcting my misprediction for a very huge error, I'm going to improve the model a lot, as compared to me predicting too.
